about.title: Two-Way Tables
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. There are five small ideas: categories, reading a table, totals, relative frequency and deciding if two things are linked. Each gets a quick check, then two practice questions at the end. If it feels rushed, stop after the 'Association' idea and do the practice in a second sitting.

say.text: Welcome to class 35. Today we link two questions about the same group of people, using one table.

show.text: Two-Way Tables

say.text: By the end, you can read one, build one, and say whether two things seem connected. We'll go one small step at a time.

show.text: Read a table | Find totals | Use percentages fairly | Decide if two things seem linked

say.text: First, a word. A categorical variable sorts people into groups, like favorite color: red, blue, green.

show.text: Categorical variable: answers that fall into groups

ask.q: Which of these is a categorical variable?
ask.why: Toppings sort people into groups, like cheese or pepperoni. The other three are numbers that we measure or count.

say.text: A two-way table compares two categorical variables. One goes across the top and the other goes down the side.

show.text: Two-way table: one variable across the top, one down the side

say.text: Our example: 24 students answered two yes-or-no questions. Do you play a sport? Do you play a musical instrument?

show.text: An empty table. Across the top: 'Sports?' with columns Yes, No, Total. Down the left side: 'Musical instrument?' with rows Yes, No, Total.

say.text: Rows run left to right. Columns run up and down. Sports answers are our columns. Instrument answers are our rows.

show.text: The same empty table. The Sports Yes column is shaded. The Instrument Yes row is shaded a different color.

ask.q: In our table, what do the two answer columns (not counting Total) stand for?
ask.right: Plays a sport: Yes, and plays a sport: No
wrong: Plays an instrument: Yes, and plays an instrument: No
Students who are 13, and students who are 14
ask.why: We put the sports question across the top, so its answers are the columns. The instrument answers run down the side as the rows.

say.text: Now fill it in. Each number inside the table is a joint frequency. It counts people who fit one pair of answers.

show.text: Filled table. Instrument Yes: Sports Yes 6, Sports No 7, Total 13. Instrument No: Sports Yes 8, Sports No 3, Total 11. Total row: 14, 10, 24.

say.text: For example, 6 students play a sport and an instrument. 7 play an instrument but no sport.

show.text: Joint frequency: the count for one pair of answers

ask.q: How many students play a sport but do not play an instrument?
ask.why: Find the column 'Sports: Yes' and the row 'Instrument: No'. They meet at 8. The 7 is the opposite pair: instrument, no sport.

say.text: The numbers on the edge are totals. We call them marginal frequencies. Each one adds up the joint frequencies in its row or column.

show.text: Marginal frequency: a row or column total

say.text: Instrument Yes row: 6 + 7 = 13. The corner number, 24, is everybody. Both the row totals and the column totals should add to it.

ask.q: How many students play a sport, whether or not they play an instrument?
ask.why: That is the total of the 'Sports: Yes' column: 6 + 8 = 14. The 24 is all students. The 6 and 8 are only parts of the sport players.

say.text: Now let's build one. This class of 20 is made up. 12 walk to school and 8 ride. Of the 12 walkers, 5 have practice after school. Of the 8 riders, 6 do.

show.text: A table being built. Rows: Walk, Ride, Total. Columns: Practice Yes, Practice No, Total. Walk: 5, 7, 12. Ride: 6, 2, 8. Total: 11, 9, 20.

say.text: Steps: put the known counts in their cells. Find each missing cell by subtracting from its row total. Then add the columns and check they reach 20.

show.text: 1. Put known counts in cells | 2. Subtract from the row total to find missing cells | 3. Add the columns | 4. Check the grand total

ask.q: How many students ride to school and have no practice?
ask.why: Riders total 8, and 6 of them have practice. So 8 - 6 = 2 do not. The 9 is everyone without practice, walkers and riders together.

say.text: Back to the 24 students. 14 play a sport and 10 don't. Those groups are different sizes, so raw counts are hard to compare.

show.text: 14 sport players vs 10 non-players

say.text: Relative frequency fixes this. It is a count shown as a fraction or percent of a total. First, a total of everyone: 6 out of 24 do both. That is 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25, or 25%.

show.text: Relative frequency: a count as a fraction or percent of a total

ask.q: What fraction of the whole group of 24 plays a sport?
ask.why: The sport total is 14 and the whole group is 24. So 14 ÷ 24 is about 0.58. The 10 out of 24 is the non-players. A part can't be 140% of the group.

say.text: Often the better question is 'among those who...'. Then we divide by that group's own total, not by 24.
Among the 14 sport players, 6 play an instrument. That is 6 ÷ 14, about 43%. This is a column relative frequency, because we used a column total.

show.text: Among a group: divide by that row's or column's total

ask.q: Of the 10 students who do NOT play a sport, 7 play an instrument. What percent is that?
ask.why: The question says 'of those who do not play a sport', so divide by that group's total, 10. 7 ÷ 10 = 0.70, which is 70%. The 29% divides by everyone, which answers a different question.

say.text: Here are both answers side by side. It's a fair comparison now, because each is a percent of its own group.

show.text: Percent who play an instrument, by sport

say.text: Among sport players, about 43% play an instrument. Among non-players, 70% do. That's a big gap.

show.text: Plays a sport: 6 of 14, about 43% | Does not play a sport: 7 of 10, 70%

say.text: When percentages differ like this, we say there seems to be an association. Knowing one answer helps you estimate the other.

show.text: Association: two variables are statistically related

say.text: In this class, sport players were less likely to play an instrument. That's called a negative association. Notice we say 'seems'. It's only a pattern in this data.

show.text: Positive association | Negative association | No association

ask.q: Which statement does the 43% versus 70% result support best?
ask.right: In this class, sport players were less likely to play an instrument, so the two seem linked.
wrong: Playing a sport makes students quit their instruments.
There is no link, because both percentages are below 100%.
There is a link, because more students play sports than don't.
ask.why: We compare the rates inside each group, and they differ. A pattern like this doesn't show one thing causes the other. Comparing raw counts of sport and non-sport players says nothing about a link.

say.text: Links aren't guaranteed, though. Sometimes the percentages match. Another made-up class of 30: 20 have pets and 10 don't.

show.text: Table. Pet Yes: Glasses Yes 6, Glasses No 14, Total 20. Pet No: Glasses Yes 3, Glasses No 7, Total 10. Total row: 9, 21, 30.

say.text: Among pet owners, 6 of 20 wear glasses: 30%. Among non-owners, 3 of 10: also 30%. The rates match, so no association.

ask.q: Which fact in the pet-and-glasses table shows there is no association?
ask.right: The glasses rate is 30% for pet owners and 30% for non-owners.
wrong: There are 20 pet owners but only 10 non-owners.
ask.why: Different group sizes and different counts don't matter. What matters is the rate inside each group, and both rates are 30%. So knowing about pets doesn't help you guess about glasses.

say.text: Your turn, with real data. A study asked 97 athletes whether they meditated before a track meet. It also asked whether they felt calm or agitated.

show.text: Table. Calm: Meditated 45, Did not meditate 8, Total 53. Agitated: Meditated 23, Did not meditate 21, Total 44. Total row: 68, 29, 97.

say.text: First, check the totals. 45 + 8 = 53 and 23 + 21 = 44. 53 + 44 = 97. Good. Now a question.

ask.q: Of the athletes who did NOT meditate, what percent felt calm?
ask.why: 'Of those who did not meditate' means the 'did not meditate' column, total 29. Calm in that column is 8, and 8 ÷ 29 is about 0.28. The 72% is the agitated share of that group.

say.text: Same trick for the meditators: 45 of 68 felt calm. That's about 66%. Here are both rates.

show.text: Percent who felt calm, by whether they meditated

say.text: Last question. Look at the 66% and the 28%, then pick the best conclusion.

show.text: Meditated: 45 of 68 calm, about 66% | Did not meditate: 8 of 29 calm, about 28%

ask.q: Which conclusion fits the meditation data best?
ask.right: Calm was more common among athletes who meditated (about 66% vs 28%), so the two seem linked.
wrong: This proves meditating makes athletes calm.
There is no link, because only 8 non-meditators were calm.
We can't compare, because the groups are different sizes (68 and 29).
ask.why: Relative frequencies cancel out the group sizes, so the comparison is fair. A big gap points to a link. A table alone can't prove one thing causes the other.

say.text: Let's gather it up. A two-way table puts two categorical variables together. The inside numbers are joint frequencies. The edge numbers are marginal frequencies.

show.text: Rows and columns, with totals | Joint frequency: inside cell | Marginal frequency: row or column total | Relative frequency: count ÷ a total

say.text: To check for a link, find the percent inside each group and compare. Quite different means a possible association. About equal means none. Next class is our course review. Well done today.

show.text: Compare the rates, not the counts

notes.topic: Relative frequency is a fraction or percent of a total, so it connects to unit rate and proportional thinking

The walking-to-school and pets-and-glasses tables are made up for practice. The music-and-sports and meditation tables come from the cited curriculum sources, and the percentages were worked out in this lesson from their counts.

other_side.claim: If the percentages differ a lot, the two categories seem linked.
other_side.other_view: A link in a table does not mean that one thing causes the other. The standard asks only for a 'possible association', and statistics texts stress that two-way tables show association, not causation. So the cautious wording is 'seems linked'.
